len.title: How str::len works
len.description: The length in bytes, which is not always the number of characters.

slides.caption: Rust strings are UTF-8. Plain letters take 1 byte; letters like é take 2.
h is 1 byte.
é is 2 bytes in UTF-8.
l, l and o are 1 byte each.
5 characters, but len() is 6. Use s.chars().count() to count characters.

chars.title: How str::chars works
chars.description: An iterator over the characters (Unicode scalar values) of a string.

slides.caption: chars() decodes the UTF-8 bytes and yields one char at a time.
'é' is one char, even though it takes 2 bytes.
chars() gives 5 items for "héllo", while len() says 6 bytes. Some symbols (like emoji with skin tones) are several chars.

char_indices.title: How str::char_indices works
char_indices.description: Each character together with its byte position.

slides.caption: char_indices yields (byte index, char) pairs. The index is where the char starts in the bytes.
'h' starts at byte 0.
'é' starts at byte 1 and takes bytes 1 and 2.
So the next 'l' starts at byte 3, not 2.
These byte indexes are the ones you may use for slicing: &s[3..] is "llo".

split.title: How str::split works
split.description: Cuts a string at every separator; empty pieces are kept.

slides.caption: split(',') cuts at every comma and yields the pieces between them.
Before the first comma: "a".
Between the first two commas: "b".
Between two commas in a row there is nothing: an empty piece "".
After the last comma: "c".
Empty pieces are kept on purpose. Add .filter(|s| !s.is_empty()) to drop them, or use split_whitespace for spaces.

split_whitespace.title: How str::split_whitespace works
split_whitespace.description: Splits at any run of spaces, tabs or newlines; never yields empty pieces.

slides.caption: split_whitespace treats any run of whitespace as one separator and ignores it at both ends.
The leading spaces are skipped.
The first word is "hi".
Three spaces in a row count as one separator.
"you", and the trailing space is ignored.
Perfect for reading words from input. Compare split(' '), which would give empty pieces here.

lines.title: How str::lines works
lines.description: Splits a string into lines; handles both \n and \r\n.

note.text: the line endings are not included

slides.caption: lines() cuts at each line ending (shown as ↵) and drops it.
The first line is "one".
The second line is "two". A final line ending does not create an empty line.
lines() also removes the \r of Windows line endings, so "a\r\nb" gives "a", "b".

trim.title: How str::trim works
trim.description: Removes whitespace from both ends; returns a slice of the same string.

slides.caption: trim finds the first and last non-whitespace characters and returns what is between them.
Leading spaces are cut off.
Trailing spaces too.
What is left is "hi": a view into the original string.
trim returns &str borrowed from the original. trim_start and trim_end cut only one side.

starts_with.title: How str::starts_with works
starts_with.description: Checks whether the string begins with a given text.

slides.caption: starts_with compares the first characters with the pattern.
The first 4 characters are "rust", exactly the pattern.
So the answer is true. The rest is not looked at.
The pattern can also be a char or a closure: s.starts_with(char::is_uppercase). ends_with checks the end.

contains.title: How str::contains works
contains.description: Checks whether a text appears anywhere in the string.

note.text: anywhere, not just at the start

slides.caption: contains searches the whole string for the pattern.
"o w" is found starting at position 4.
contains only says whether it exists: true.
Use find to also learn where it is. The search is case-sensitive: "Hello".contains("hello") is false.

find.title: How str::find works
find.description: Returns the byte index where a pattern first appears.

note.text: the first match from the left

slides.caption: find looks for "an" from the left and returns where the first match starts.
At index 0, "ba" is not "an".
At index 1, "an" matches: the answer is Some(1).
rfind searches from the right ("banana".rfind("an") is Some(3)). None means not found.

split_once.title: How str::split_once works
split_once.description: Splits at the first separator into exactly two parts.

slides.caption: split_once cuts at the first separator only and returns the part before and the part after.
The first = is at index 3. Before it: "key".
Everything after it is the second part, including the second =.
Ideal for "key=value" lines. Without a separator it returns None. rsplit_once cuts at the last one.

splitn.title: How str::splitn works
splitn.description: Splits at most into n pieces; the last piece keeps the rest.

slides.caption: splitn(2, ...) makes at most one cut, so there are at most 2 pieces.
The first piece: "a".
That was the one allowed cut: the rest stays together, dashes included.
splitn(1, x) never cuts at all.

parse.title: How str::parse works
parse.description: Converts text into another type; returns a Result because it can fail.

slides.caption: parse reads the text and tries to build the type you ask for, here i32.
"42" is a valid number: Ok(42).
"4x" is not: Err, with a ParseIntError explaining why.
Handle the Result: "42".parse::<i32>()? in a function, or .unwrap_or(0) for a default. Spaces are not allowed: trim first.

strip_prefix.title: How str::strip_prefix works
strip_prefix.description: Removes a prefix if it is there; returns None if it is not.

slides.caption: strip_prefix checks the start and returns the rest only when the prefix matches.
The string starts with 'v': it is removed.
The rest is returned: Some("1.2.3").
If the prefix is missing you get None, so you know. trim_start_matches would silently do nothing (or remove several).

get.title: How str::get works
get.description: Slices safely by byte range: None instead of a panic.

slides.caption: Byte 2 is in the middle of é (bytes 1 and 2). Slicing there would cut a character in half.
Bytes 0..2 would be h plus half of é.
&s[0..2] would panic. get(0..2) returns None instead.
get(0..3) is Some("hé"). When ranges come from char_indices, they always fall on boundaries.

bytes.title: How str::bytes works
bytes.description: An iterator over the raw UTF-8 bytes of a string.

slides.caption: bytes() yields the u8 values that store the string.
'h' is stored as the byte 104.
'é' takes two bytes: 195 and 169.
Use bytes() for ASCII data or byte-level work; chars() for text.

trim_start.title: How str::trim_start works
trim_start.description: Removes whitespace at the start only.

slides.caption: trim_start cuts whitespace from the beginning.
The two leading spaces are cut off.
The trailing spaces stay.
trim_end does the other side; trim does both.

trim_end.title: How str::trim_end works
trim_end.description: Removes whitespace at the end only, such as a trailing newline.

slides.caption: Lines read from input often end with a newline (↵). trim_end removes it.
The newline at the end is whitespace: removed.
"ok" is left.
Always trim input before parsing: "42\n".parse::<i32>() fails, "42" works.

ends_with.title: How str::ends_with works
ends_with.description: Checks whether the string ends with a given text.

slides.caption: ends_with compares the last characters with the pattern.
The last 4 characters are ".png".
So the answer is true.
Case matters: "PHOTO.PNG".ends_with(".png") is false. For paths, std::path::Path::extension is more robust.

rfind.title: How str::rfind works
rfind.description: The byte index of the last match of a pattern.

slides.caption: rfind finds the last occurrence, but the index still counts from the left.
Searching from the right, the first / found is at index 3.
The other / at index 1 is never reached.
To take everything after it: &s[i + 1..] is "c". rsplit_once('/') does both in one step.

strip_suffix.title: How str::strip_suffix works
strip_suffix.description: Removes a suffix if it is there; None if it is not.

slides.caption: strip_suffix checks the end and returns the part before it.
".txt" is at the end: removed.
Some("report") is returned.
Returns None when the suffix is missing, so you can tell the two cases apart.

rsplit_once.title: How str::rsplit_once works
rsplit_once.description: Splits at the last separator into two parts.

slides.caption: rsplit_once cuts at the last separator.
The last . is before "gz".
Before it: "archive.tar". After it: "gz".
split_once('.') would give ("archive", "tar.gz") instead.

matches.title: How str::matches works
matches.description: An iterator over every match of a pattern.

slides.caption: matches yields every piece of the string that matches the pattern.
"1" matches.
And "3".
With a string pattern, s.matches("ab").count() counts how often "ab" appears (without overlaps).

eq_ignore_ascii_case.title: How str::eq_ignore_ascii_case works
eq_ignore_ascii_case.description: Compares two strings, treating upper and lower case ASCII letters as equal.

slides.caption: Each pair of characters is compared after lowering A–Z.
Y/y, e/E, s/S: equal when case is ignored.

eq.text: y = y, e = e, s = s

slides.caption: All pairs match: true.
Cheaper than a.to_lowercase() == b.to_lowercase(), which allocates two Strings.
